title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: More general guidence can be found here: Generative AI Hub | Teaching & Learning - UCL – University College London Select activity Questions and General posts Questions and General posts Forum Select section Weekly Activity Sequences Collapse Expand Weekly Activity Sequences Overview There are four major activities in each week of DUTE_AI. 1) Complete core reading materials and pre-recorded lectures for the week. Every week there will be core readings (including further reading suggestions) and may be some pre-recorded lectures. Please aim to finish them before the class . 2) Participate in a debate on the Moodle Forum Every week, you will be asked to join an online debate on a weekly proposed argument regarding the promises and challenges of educational technologies. You could either add comments for or against a weekly proposed argument using evidence from your readings, lectures, or personal experiences. Please engage in a debate on the Moodle Forum before the class ( 5 PM on Thursday UK time ). Each week, you will receive an AI-generated first post when the weekly course content is released. These posts will be shared using the account named Yildiz Uzun . 3) Attend a live class for the lectures and group activities Every week, a face-to-face class will be held at the room-G2 in the Knowledge Lab on Thursday at 5:00 PM (UK time) .

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: The live class comprises (1) a lecture (~90 mins) to answer some of the questions that you may have from the weekly materials, followed by (2) group activities (~90 mins). Throughout the module, you will be working on some learning analytics and AI tasks individually. In addition, you will work as a group on a data analytics project to tackle an educational problem. In relation to the weekly lecture content, there will be tasks for you and your team to complete on Python Notebooks and Miro. Note: After interdisciplinary groups are formed based on your survey information, you will be invited to your group activity board on Miro. Please create an account on Miro using your real name and use the template to complete weekly group activities. For remote students, please see an additional guideline here . 4) Reflect on Google Docs At the end of the week, you are expected to write your individual reflections on the weekly content/activities via a single Google Docs file. These reflections will be guided by specific questions posed each week. Please share your single Google Docs with us: Qi Zhou (qtnvqz3@ucl.ac.uk) Wannapon Suraworachet (wannapon.suraworachet.20@ucl.ac.uk) Yildiz Uzun ( yildiz.uzun.22@ucl.ac.uk ) with editing access (editor) directly through emails. This only needs to be done once. Here is general guidance on writing academic reflections.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: The following document demonstrates a guideline for reflective content. Select activity Individual reflection guideline Individual reflection guideline File DOCX Done You must Done: View 66.0 KB Select activity PartA_IndividualReflection_Example1 PartA_IndividualReflection_Example1 File PDF 58.7 KB Select activity PartA_IndividualReflection_Example2 PartA_IndividualReflection_Example2 File PDF 65.0 KB Select section EducAItional Challenge Group Activity Collapse Expand EducAItional Challenge Group Activity Throughout the module, you will be assigned to a group, and you will be asked to design, prototype, and evaluate machine learning solutions to address real-world educational challenges. This section covers information about how to approach the group work task. Select activity EducAItional Challenge Group Activity Overview EducAItional Challenge Group Activity Overview Page Select activity Design Cases Design Cases Page Select section FAQ Collapse Expand FAQ This section attempts to answer any questions that you may have. Learning Materials When will the new week’s materials be released? They are released every Monday for the following Thursday’s class. Should I complete the video lectures and the essential reading before the class starts? Yes, we are expecting you to prepare yourself before engaging with the class and the group activities.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: These materials are aimed to supply you with sufficient information to support your contributions during the class. How can I have access to manuscripts, chapters, books etc.? We are providing links to many readings. But, for others, you can search for articles using the UCL Explore library service: Go to Explore → Please see the instruction here: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/library/finding-resources/electronic-resources/about-explore The Debate activity Is this mandatory? We strongly encourage you to contribute to the debate activity. It is also part of the attendance requirements, which requires you to engage with at least 80% of the module activities. When is the deadline for this activity? You are suggested to participate in the debate before the class starts on Thursday evenings. However, you can also respond to peers after class. Q&A sessions with the module instructor(s) Is this mandatory? Q&A sessions for online students are not mandatory. However, this session aims to open-up relevant discussion on the module content and help clarify questions that you might have so we suggest that you join us (besides they are often quite fun sessions!). Will the Q&A sessions be recorded? Yes, we will provide the link to the recordings afterwards. What if I missed the session? This is perfectly fine.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: If you have a question and couldn’t ask it during the session, you can always pose a question in the Moodle forum to ask us any time. Group Project Do we have to create the design solution? No, we only expect you to present the conceptual ideas of your design solution without a need to actually create one. However, you could include the prototypes of your design solution in the final presentation, if you have already started working on them. Does the group project count as a part of the grade? Yes, this activity is mainly aimed to help you develop an in-depth understanding of the contents through applied knowledge and collaboration. Both individual reflection portfolio and the critical essay submissions which are evaluated are directly related to your group work interactions, so doing a good job for your group work will matter for your grade. Does the Miro record count as a part of the grade? We do not directly assess it. The tasks are designed to fuel you towards an understanding of the topic at hand and prepare you for your weekly reflections and the final submission. When will the presentation take place? In week 10, each group will present their design solutions case to the class. Groups can choose to present their idea in person or through a recorded video.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: What is to be covered in the presentation? We are expecting you to present a sensible flow of the weekly activities and developments that lead to your proposed solution to an educational challenge. Do I need to submit the presentation before the presentation day? Yes, you are asked to submit your group presentation or video recording the day before the presentation day at 3 pm UK time. What will happen on the presentation day? Each group will have 10 minutes to present, followed by 5 mins of a Q&A session. After every group has completed, everyone will vote for the top 3 design cases. The top team will receive a small gift from the module team. The voting system is only available synchronously during class time. Therefore, some remote students might not have a chance to cast their vote if they do not attend the session live. Weekly-surveys Where can I access them? Please create an account on the DUTE_AI App before logging in to submit your response. You might find this introduction to the app useful. Is this mandatory? They are not. This activity aims for students to reflect on their own conditions and possibly on other members’ conditions to foster group discussion and promote shared understanding within the group. What kind of data is collected? The app only collects data about your email, your name and your group number.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: These data are stored in a real-time database (firebase) for the duration of your study for teaching and research purposes only and not shared further, deleted immediately after. Apart from the surveys that you’ve submitted, the app also collects your log activity such as logging in/out, page viewing, and responses to the final survey questions. Please speak to a DUTE_AI team member if you have any questions. When should I fill in the surveys? The post-survey is expected to be completed right after the group discussion ended. However, both of the surveys will accept the responses at other times as well. Can I edit my response? Currently, it is not possible to edit your responses. Please submit another response, we will consider the latest one as your intended response. Who else can see my survey results? Your surveys are only shared with your teammates to promote shared understanding. Can I see my own response? You are able to the follow-up plans from the surveys by selecting the 'My weekly goals/plan' from the menubar. If I find errors in the app, what should I do? Please send an email to wannapon.suraworachet.20@ucl.ac.uk , describing your process where it led to the errors and attaching a screenshot(s) of the errors. We will contact you to resolve the issue asap.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: Attendance requirements How is this calculated? UCL expects you to attend all scheduled teaching events and to be actively engaged in at least 80% of the module activities. The engagement is measured from your contributions to the debate activity, group discussions and the individual interaction data with the learning materials. What will happen if I have to leave early for some weeks? You are advised to inform the Module leader and the Teaching assistants when you are unable to attend a scheduled teaching event, or have to leave early. Moreover, for the module activities that are designed to be both synchronous and asynchronous, you can go back and complete any incomplete tasks at your preferred time. If you will not be able to attend multiple sessions, please submit a formal request for Extenuating Circumstances to the Department. Please see: https://www.ucl.ac.uk/academic-manual/chapters/chapter-2-student-support-framework/section-2-short-term-illness-and-other-extenuating Assessment Where can I find the example essays? Please see under this section: example essays What are the marking criteria? Please see: Marking Criteria File What is the referencing style? APA style is strongly suggested but any referencing style is acceptable, as long as it is consistently applied.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: Please refer to this page for more info: https://library-guides.ucl.ac.uk/APA What would happen if the Turnitin results say that my final report is highly similar to my draft submission? Does it influence my final assessment? This wouldn't influence your final assessment as we can also see the similarity is with your own draft and differs from others’ work. Part A Individual Reflection What should be covered in my individual reflection? In general, we are expecting you to reflect upon your learning experiences with the module ranging from the individual, group and cohort activities. We also provided weekly prompts under the weekly materials which you can consider while reflecting. However, please remember to cover the reflective contents across learning activities for each week. We are keen to know what you have learnt and how this has influenced your thinking, not a mere description of what happened during the class. How many words for the individual reflection weekly? You are expected to provide a weekly reflection of approximately 300-500 words. However, the length of the document here is only a guideline as we don’t limit reflective writing. Longer writings for exceeding 500 words per week will only be evaluated for up to 500 words. Writing succinctly is an important skill to develop.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: There is no merit in lengthy submissions per se, but if you need space for more, the reasons why your reflections are greater than the suggested number of words should be justifiable. Can I include a diagram(s) in the reflection document? Yes if it helps convey your message. Do I need to add references to my individual reflections? Yes, where possible, to show evidence for your arguments. How should I share this part to receive feedback? Is there a deadline for this ? Please use GoogleDocs as a documenting platform and share the document with teaching assistants as ‘editors’ via email once you created the document: Qi Zhou (qtnvqz3@ucl.ac.uk) Wannapon Suraworachet (wannapon.suraworachet.20@ucl.ac.uk) Yildiz Uzun ( yildiz.uzun.22@ucl.ac.uk ) Please update the contents weekly on the same document to receive analytics feedback. We will get in touch in case we have a problem with your document. Since teaching assistants will provide formative feedback (in-text comments) as well during the reading week (week 6), it is suggested to keep your document updated by the time. However, this is optional. The final deadline for the summative assessment is the same deadline as Part B. Can we revise it after receiving the comments? We expect you to take the feedback on board and revise the contents of your reflection accordingly before the final deadline.

title: Week 10: EducAItional Challenge and Student Presentations (w/c 08 Dec)
text: Do I need to create a new Google account for this? You can either use your personal email or create a new google account using UCL email for this task specifically. In case you use your personal email, please make sure that we know who you are by including your name in the email or the document. Which weeks are optional for reflection?

text: Week 1 and week 10 are optional for individual reflections What is the format of the reflection document? When is the last day for editing my reflections? During the term, there is no specific format for the reflection other than the content and length to receive formative and analytics feedback. However, you need to submit your final version to the Moodle with your Part B- design critique, following the submission criteria. Part B Design Critique What should be covered in the critical essay? Is it acceptable to choose one or two topics from the module (i.e. learning analytics, value-driven nature of data and algorithms, multimodal learning analytics, orchestration etc.) to go deeper into? We anticipate coverage of all the topics delivered in DUTE_AI. However, it is perfectly normal that some weeks' content will be covered more in-depth, whereas some others will be more briefly mentioned. Do I have to state which option I choose? Not necessarily. We can infer this from your essay. Option B.1 extending the group design case to a new problem: should I briefly describe my existing design? Yes, as your essay is expected to be complete on its own. Please make sure that you include the necessary information on the existing design before starting to expand the design case.

title: Week 1 and week 10 are optional for individual reflections
text: However, please note that what is expected is your critical evaluation of this new case rather than a descriptive discussion of the extension work. Option B.2 critique of a technology design (commercial or academic) with respect to its educational value: Do I have to elaborate on whether I pick a commercial EdTech or an academic EdTech? Not necessarily. You don't need to distinguish and try to build an argument whether the educational technology you are critiquing is an academic or a commercial one in your essay. We provide these options to keep students' opportunities wide so that everyone can write a critical essay on an EdTech they are genuinely interested in. The boundaries between the two are not very straightforward to draw. Many EdTech products start as academic/research products and can be later on commercialised (i.e Duolingo). Before the module lectures start, please pay attention to the following resources and activities that we've prepared for you. Educational Technologies are important tools that can give teachers and learners a great deal of insight into the learning process. As much as we argue for the potential of educational technologies to support learning, we also think that all systems and decisions within educational technology implementations should be transparent to their users. Therefore, it is important that you know exactly what data you are generating through the technologies you are using in this module, how such data is utilised, and what kind of support we aim to provide you with the use of data. text: Week 3: Richard Noss Lecture (w/c 13 Oct) Richard Noss Lecture 2025- Professor Manu Kapur "Learning Through Productive Failure In The GenAI Age" If learning from failure is intuitively compelling, why do we wait for it to happen. Why don’t we intentionally design for it, and harness it for deep learning? In his talk, Prof. Kapur will describe what Productive Failure is, how, when and why intentionally designing for failure in a safe way can lead to deep learning, and its implications for how we can design powerful learning environments for developing conceptual understanding, creativity, and transfer. Prof. Manu Kapur's lecture will be followed by a panel discussion: Panel Title: Human Learning and Generative AI: Neurocognitive Foundations, Pedagogical Innovation, & Technical Frontiers This panel will examine how generative AI is impacting higher education by interrogating the neurocognitive mechanisms underpinning learning, exploring genAI as a catalyst for learning and metacognition, and addressing the technical and research challenges in designing GenAI systems for nuanced pedagogical support for learning. Drawing on research and practice examples from UCL, ETH and beyond, panellists will debate what higher education should emphasise, how we scaffold learning, and what innovations are still needed. In this week's lecture, we will focus on multiple modalities that can be taken into account to provide continued support for learning across physical and digital spaces.

text: Week 6: Value-driven Nature of Data and Performance Measures (w/c 10 Nov) Value-driven Nature of Data and Algorithms: This session will discuss the value-driven nature of artefacts including data and algorithms and will cover some methodologies to measure the success and failure of learning analytics models in practice. title: Week 6: Value-driven Nature of Data and Performance Measures (w/c 10 Nov)
text: This week, we will investigate the 'politics' of educational technologies and discuss the potential underlying values that shape the design and use of technology in education. Using case study examples, we will build up the arguments for potential values that could/should be driving educational technologies for learning. In addition, we will cover common AI model performance metrics and highlight many design decisions taken while deciding about what models are best for educational contexts. Elaborations on the multiple design decisions taken on AI performance evaluations aim to give insights into the value-laden nature of AI models in Education. 4) Team Discussion on your group design case This week you will be asked to compare performance of the models built in earlier week using performance metrics introduced this week. Please see the scripts here: W6 Group activities - scripts . You will also asked to discuss values and common critiques of the DUTE_AI Teacher Dashboard and documented them on Miro. 5) Individual reflection Building upon the prediction models you encountered in earlier weeks, what predictions do you plan to generate in your design case and how you will measure their value quantitatively? You can reflect on the model performance achieved in your design case.

text: Week 7: From Prediction to Generation | Natural Language Processing in Education (w/c 17 Nov) From Prediction to Generation | Natural Language Processing (NLP) in Education: Building on the previous week’s prediction models, this session extends predictive thinking to analyse and generate text-based data through Natural Language Processing. We introduce how machines represent language—from BoW and TF-IDF to embeddings and LLMs—and compare their performance on educational tasks such as essay scoring. Learning Outcomes To understand the fundamentals of natural language processing, how machines process and represent language, from traditional NLP (BoW, TF-IDF, word2vec) to modern LLMs, and how they have been used for educational tasks. To learn key NLP techniques, including preprocessing and embeddings for analysing and generating educational text data. Practical Skills: Structure Discovery and Information Generation Building basic NLP pipelines with BoW, TF-IDF, and Word2Vec (Recurrent Neural Network). text: Week 9: Evidence-informed Implementations of AI in Education (w/c 01 Dec) Evidence-informed Implementations of AI in Education: This session will cover the importance of generating evidence about the effectiveness of AI implementations in education, challenges associated with evaluating the performance of generative AI tool implementations, and learn about how to evaluate generative AI in Education for interventions. Learning Outcomes Develop a broader understanding of the concepts of 'evidence' and 'evidence-informed education' Prepare and interpret logic models of genAI in Education interventions Develop an understanding of biases in generative AI and conduct a benchmarking study to systematically evaluate their presence and impact Practical Skills: Benchmarking Generative AI Draft a logic model on how to evaluate its impact Select activity OverviewKey Activities1) Reading taskPlease access... title: Week 9: Evidence-informed Implementations of AI in Education (w/c 01 Dec)
text: The evaluation of educational technologies is important for their impacts to be effectively integrated into learning and teaching settings to bring the best benefit to learners and teachers. However, the impact evaluations of technology in education are challenging and what is 'evidence' in educational contexts is not an easy question to answer. These challenges are more significant for emerging technologies with genAI models. In this week's lecture, we will discuss the complexities of evaluating the impact of an AI intervention in Education. 4) Team Discussion on your group design case This week, you are asked to meet with your group and conduct a benchmarking study to evaluate genAI performance. Also, you will use a logic model to evaluate the potential solution of your group design case solution with AI. 5) Individual reflection What have you learned about the importance of generating evidence for the effectiveness of AI implementations in education? What challenges do you foresee in evaluating the performance of generative AI tools in education? Reflect on how the GenAI assistant implemented on DUTEApp shaped your engagement with the analytics feedback, drawing on the ideas about evidence-informed AI in Education and the challenges of evaluating GenAI.

title: There is an increasing emphasis on ‘evidence‐based teaching’ and 'evidence-based education'. The evaluation of education
text: Week 9: Evidence-informed Implementations of AI in Education (w/c 01 Dec) There is an increasing emphasis on ‘evidence‐based teaching’ and 'evidence-based education'. The evaluation of educational technologies is important for their impacts to be effectively integrated into learning and teaching settings to bring the best benefit to learners and teachers. However, the impact evaluations of technology in education are challenging and what is 'evidence' in educational contexts is not an easy question to answer. These challenges are more significant for emerging technologies with genAI models. In this week's lecture, we will discuss the complexities of evaluating the impact of an AI intervention in Education.

text: Guidance All assessment for DUTE_AI follows the assessment guidance covered in the Programme Handbook for Staff and Students (available on the MA Education and Technology Programme Hub page on Moodle). Any questions about the general assessment regulations or the assessment for this module can be directed to the Programme Leader, or the DUTE_AI Module Leader. Students are responsible for reading and understanding all of the content in the Programme Handbook as well as the Module Handbook here . Academic Writing Statement Pieces of work are marked in accordance with the marking criteria. There is no bell curve of marks or limits on the numbers of particular grades. Each piece is marked individually. Students are advised to take very careful note of the marking criteria used for DUTE_AI below. Students are welcomed and encouraged to write in the first person (i.e. to use I think...). Personal opinions are valid contributions but must be understood as only one person's experience and viewpoint, and thus cannot stand as a sole piece of evidence for an argument. Although APA style is strongly suggested, any referencing style is acceptable, as long as it is consistently applied. If you are unsure of referencing, please consult the provided guide. The final submission of work in Part A has no total word limit, but it is recommended to keep each week's reflections to around 500 words.

The markers try very hard to mark and provide sensible feedback within a reasonable timeframe. Wordcounts help us to do this - so please don't go over! Assignment You must submit a single Microsoft Word document as the final assignment including the coversheets for Part A and Part B as the first four pages of your assignment followed by Part A and Part B. Use the coversheet file provided above this submission box. Do not use any coversheets that you have previously used for other assignments. All submissions must conform to these requirements: Submit as a Microsoft Word document. Written work needs to be in a font size 12 and in New Times Roman font. 1.5 line spacing. Include page numbers. Include a word count (please note that the word count excludes the abstract, footnotes, bibliography/references list, appendices and title). Remove any track changes or comments from the assignment. You must tick the student declaration box confirming that this is your work. This is a UCL requirement. title: Module Summary
text: Module Summary Through a mixture of theoretical and practical insights, the Design and Use of AI in Education (DUTE_AI) module offers multiple different perspectives on AI and technology design and use for education. Technology as a construct is explored in its broadest terms to allow students to appreciate its continuous presence and role in the evolution of human cognition and both practical and intellectual innovation. However, the particular focus of the module is on learning analytics tools, approaches and technologies. Pertinent theoretical perspectives of learning are summarised to provide the grounding necessary for understanding different technological designs and implementations and to furnish students with an informed basis for critiquing and evaluating technologies as educational tools in varied contexts of use. DUTE_AI module covers literature from learning analytics, AI in Education, and the learning sciences as well as the common statistical and machine learning approaches for educational data in real-world settings. In addition, the module discusses data-informed decision-making in the design and implementation of educational technologies as well as their evaluation in terms of their efficacy in achieving their intended educational outcomes in real-world contexts. Students will be engaging in all three social planes of learning.

title: Module Summary
text: 1) At the cohort level, students will engage in weekly discussions on the most significant promises and challenges of educational technologies. 2) At the group level, students will work in interdisciplinary groups to construct their own potential solutions to significant educational challenges. Design solutions will be discussed in weekly face-to-face group activities and zoom calls through brainstorming and prototyping activities. 3) At the individual level, students will work on a shared Python code to run their analyses and models, and document their individual reflections about the weekly content covered in the module. Students will use and experience some of the cutting-edge educational technologies as part of their engagement with the module as a way of promoting reflection on the current technology-enhanced learning practices.

title: Module Aims
text: Module Aims The overarching aim of this module is to 1) help students develop a comprehensive understanding of how big data and analytics are utilised to support and enhance learning experiences, 2) help students design, prototype, and evaluate machine learning solutions to address real-world educational challenges, considering the complexities of educational contexts and the orchestration of learning environments. They will develop skills in prototyping models, using API integrations, and evaluating their impact in educational settings.

title: Intended Learning Outcomes
text: Intended Learning Outcomes By the end of the module the students will be able to: Appraise critically different AI and Analytics models in a variety of different learning and teaching contexts; Engage in an interdisciplinary design process in a way that bridges between research, design and practice of machine learning use cases in education; Generate multifaceted and targeted questions of pertinence to AI in education.

title: Overview
text: Overview The assignment has two parts. Part A focuses on your weekly individual reflections over the course of the DUTE_AI module. Make sure you answer the specific questions posed each week. Part B gives you a chance to demonstrate your in-depth understanding of the content covered and knowledge developed during the module. Following the IOE policy, your assignment should be 5000 words +/- 10%. Part A will be considered equivalent to 2500 words (not equal to, so your individual reflections can add up to more than 2500 words). Part B will be equal to 2500 words in length. Your assignment should include a critical analysis of the key issues related to the design process and concepts as experienced through your group work and given your personal and research-informed reflections.

title: Part A: Critical Analysis and Reflection Portfolio
text: Part A: Critical Analysis and Reflection Portfolio For this part, your weekly individual reflections will be submitted. Please see below for guidance on what your reflections portfolio should address. Describe, support with literature, and critically reflect on the weekly content of the module, as well as the practical application of this content in weekly activities. Your priority should be to address the questions posed every week in your individual reflections. In addition to these, if applicable, you can include visual illustrations in your text as figures to support your points. It is expected that some of the reflections that you present in this part of the assignment will have been brought up during the group work and class discussions. However, the reflection of these discussions in relation to how they advance digital learning design should be your own . If you include comments and reflections made by others in the group, you must reference them as such explicitly. If you include reflections on the nature of your group work, it is important that you take a constructive stance and connect it to the literature to explain why and how the group work proceeded in the way it did.

title: Part B: Design Case Extension or Design Critique
text: Part B: Design Case Extension or Design Critique 2,500 words essay submitted. For your essay, you have two options. Option 1: Extending the group design case to a new problem Relying on the group design, consider if you would define the educational challenge differently. Explain your answer with reference to relevant research and a critique of the strengths and weaknesses of the group design. This critique ought to include strengths and weaknesses related to the type and functionality of the solution proposed as well as methods considered by the group to inform the design and development of the solution. What would you have done differently and why? What other methods might you have used or perhaps in addition to the ones considered in class to improve the design case solutions? Back your arguments with reference to research as well as specific examples of data analysis.

title: Part B: Design Case Extension or Design Critique
text: Key areas you may want to consider: What are the characteristics of the new take on the challenge addressed – is there a different domain, a different way of learning and teaching? What are the nuances of the new context of use? How (in)flexible is your design in supporting these characteristics and why? Does your new problem require revisiting your original theoretical underpinnings and why? Do the target learners need further/more detailed data to be supported? What new knowledge, if any, would you have to model in the new design? What are the open design questions for your new design? What design processes and methods will you employ to help you achieve the changes in your solution, and why? Be clear what you will learn from applying each method and how it will inform different aspects of your solution. Option 2: Critique of a data-driven technology (including AI) with respect to its educational value. Consider an existing data-driven technology, either commercially available or a research environment and critique it with respect to its educational value (examples will be posted on Moodle). You will be expected to define what you mean by the educational value with reference to existing research.

title: Part B: Design Case Extension or Design Critique
text: Consider whose perspective you are presenting in defining what may be the educational value of the technology you have chosen (learners, educators, parents, schools policy makers etc.). What are the component parts of the technology you are critiquing that may or may not contribute to it being of educational value? What are the theoretical underpinnings if any that the given technology is based and what is the evidence that motivates its design and evaluation? Key areas you may want to consider: How does the technology you are critiquing enhance learning and/or teaching? Who are the intended users of the technology you describe and w hat is the context of use for which it is intended? What are the common critiques of the data-driven technology you proposed in the literature? What are the educational aspirations on which the technology is built? What were the methods that were used to drive the data collection, analysis, and modelling decisions and how are they manifest in the design? What evidence is there of the educational value claimed? To what extent can we trust the evidence presented? How it can be further improved to enhance teaching and learning practices?

title: The core elements of academic reflective writing
text: The core elements of academic reflective writing Academic reflective writing is a genre and just like an essay has characteristics, so does academic reflective writing. Academic reflective writing requires critical and analytic thought, a clear line of argument, and the use of evidence through examples of personal experiences and thoughts and often also theoretical literature. You should aim for a balance between personal experience, tone, and academic practice and rigor. Academic reflective writing should: develop a perspective or line of reasoning develop a link between your experience or practice and existing knowledge (theoretical or personal) show understanding and appreciation of different perspectives to your own show recognition that your own understanding is likely not be complete and situations are rarely clear-cut and simplistic show learning resulting from the reflection (either by discovering something new or confirming existing knowledge) and how you plan to use it be written in an appropriate style with language relevant to your academic discipline sometimes, but not always, use theoretical literature to inform your understanding. People can have misconceptions about academic reflective writing – some of the common ones are described below.

title: The core elements of academic reflective writing
text: Academic reflective writing is NOT… Instead… Just descriptions of what has happened Descriptions should be used as foundations for learning. A personal diary where you can say anything and use any language Academic reflective writing require structure and formal language. A place where you get marks for self-disclosure – while reflection is personal, you will not get a good mark by merely sharing challenging experiences or personal trauma The experiences you share must be used actively to promote learning AND be appropriate for the audience. An assessor will probably not be comfortable reading your darkest secrets. Private reflections may include such content, but for academic refection it is unlikely to be appropriate. Reflections should be appropriate both for your boundaries and the boundaries of the person reading them. A place where you get marks for complementing the course or teacher assessing you Include the course and the teacher if they have affected you, but be sure to uncover what about them worked or did not work for you, and how you can use this knowledge in other contexts. A place where you reference learning uncritically You should evidence how you have learned something, what it means for you, and how it will be used in the future.

title: Referencing & Plagiarism
text: Referencing & Plagiarism When finalising any written assignment, these please remember that, to avoid plagiarism, it is essential that you pay proper attention to referencing and the use of citations. Plagiarism is taken very seriously at the UCL IOE. Please remember that: All direct quotations from another author's work must be placed in quotation marks and cited correctly by providing the author name, date, and page number. All data, ideas, or lines of argument, which you appropriate from another author (even if you do not use their exact words), must be acknowledged and referenced correctly. You also need to ensure you do not plagiarise your own work (self-plagiarism). You cannot include material that you have written and submitted for another assignment without referencing it correctly. Further information about avoiding plagiarism can be found in the Programme Handbook (available on the Programme Handbook Moodle site). In addition to revising these guidelines, we strongly recommend that you run your assignments through a test Turnitin drop box before you submit them. To do this please visit https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/enrol/index.php?id=12731 and log in with your UCL username and password.
